samples.question: The picture shows eight upright coloured bars on a plain background: two red bars, two blue bars, two green bars and two purple bars. The two bars that share a colour form one pair, and colour alone says which two bars belong together; the two bars of one pair are always drawn near each other with plain background between them, and each pair keeps to its own part of the page. All bars are drawn with the same width; only their lengths differ. The bars float freely, so they do not stand on any shared baseline and the length of a bar is how long the bar itself is, not how high or how low it sits on the page. Score a pair by the length of its shorter bar: the pair's score is the length of whichever of its two bars is the shorter one, so a pair with one very long bar and one short bar scores badly. Exactly one pair has a strictly greater score than every other pair. The single longest bar in the whole picture always belongs to one of the losing pairs, so the answer is never the colour of the longest bar. Which pair holds more coloured ink in total, where each pair sits on the page, which bar of a pair is drawn on the upper left and which on the lower right, how far apart the two bars of a pair are, and the small grey specks scattered in the background all carry no information. Which coloured pair has the longest shorter bar? Answer with one of: red, blue, green, purple.
